title: Was America Founded as a Christian Nation?
subtitle: The strongest case for yes, the strongest case for no, and the deeper question both sides forget to ask.

sections.title: Why the Question Burns
sections.body:
You have heard it both ways, and you have heard it loud. On one side, a confident assertion that America was built on the Bible, that the founders knelt before they wrote, that the country is a covenant nation drifting from its first love. On the other side, an equally confident denial that the founders were mostly skeptics, that the Constitution is a secular document, that the whole story was invented later by people who wanted to wrap the Bible in a flag. Both sides argue as if the past were a weapon, because it is.

The question is not really about 1776. It is about now. Whoever owns the founding owns the argument about what the country owes God, about whose vision of the public square is legitimate, about whether a Christian asking for a place at the table is reclaiming an inheritance or imposing a creed. That is why people fight over a phrase that none of the founders used about themselves. The stakes are present. The evidence is past. And the temptation on every side is to read the second in light of the first.

I want to refuse that temptation, and I want to confess at the start that my own tradition has not refused it. Christians have reached for this claim when we felt our influence slipping, and we have reached for it in a way that says more about our anxiety than about our history. So this is not a neutral exercise for me. It is partly a reckoning. Before we can answer the question well, we have to want the truth more than we want the verdict.

sections.title: The Case for Yes
sections.body:
Take the strongest version, not the bumper sticker. The English colonies were planted, in large part, by people whose every assumption was Christian. John Winthrop stood on the deck of the Arbella in 1630 and called his colony a city upon a hill, lifting the phrase straight from the Sermon on the Mount, casting New England as a people in covenant with God under the eye of the watching world. That image did not die in Massachusetts. It became part of how the country imagined itself, and it was Christian to its roots.

Most of the ideas at the founding came out of the church. It was just the air. The conviction that rulers are accountable to a higher law, that conscience cannot be coerced, that human beings are fallen and therefore power must be divided and checked, came down through Calvinist political thought and a century of Puritan argument. The Declaration of Independence grounds human equality not in the state but in the Creator, asserting that all men are endowed by their Creator with certain unalienable rights. Strip the Creator out and the sentence loses its floor. Rights that come from God cannot be repealed by a king, and that was precisely the point.

The founders themselves, whatever their private creeds, lived and spoke inside a biblical world. They quoted Scripture in debate, declared days of fasting and thanksgiving, opened Congress with prayer. The language of Providence runs through Washington and even through Franklin, who proposed prayer at the Constitutional Convention. The common people of the new nation were overwhelmingly churchgoing Protestants whose moral vocabulary, whose sense of sin and judgment and mercy, came from the pulpit. To call this a Christian culture is not propaganda. It is description. The historian who denies the depth of that influence is hiding from the record.

sections.title: The Case for No
sections.body:
Now take the other side at its strongest, and it is strong. The men who wrote the founding documents were children of the Enlightenment as much as of the church. Jefferson edited the miracles out of his Gospels with a razor. Franklin doubted the divinity of Christ. Many of the most important founders were Deists or heterodox theists who spoke of Nature and Nature is God, of Providence and the Author of our being, in language that left Christ out. A culture can be Christian while its architects are not, and these architects often were not.

Then there is the document itself. The Constitution of 1787 is, on the question of God, silent. It contains no mention of Jesus, no invocation of Scripture, no claim of national covenant. Its only reference to religion is a prohibition, Article Six, which forbids any religious test for public office. The First Amendment opens by barring Congress from establishing religion and from prohibiting its free exercise. The founders had the religious establishments of Europe in full view, and the bloodshed they produced, and they chose deliberately to build a government that did not rest on a confession. That was not an oversight. It was the design.

The sharpest single line comes from the Treaty of Tripoli, ratified unanimously by the Senate in 1797 and signed by John Adams, which states plainly that the Government of the United States is not in any sense founded on the Christian religion. And there is the contradiction that no honest account can skip. A nation calling itself Christian held millions of human beings as property, wrote the protection of slavery into its founding compact, and counted the enslaved as three fifths of a person. If the tree is known by its fruit, the fruit indicts the claim. A country that crucifies the image of God in chains has no clean title to the name of Christ.

sections.title: The Honest Verdict
sections.body:
Both confident answers are wrong because both confuse two different things. There is influence, and there is establishment. America was profoundly shaped by Christianity. America was not founded as a Christian nation in any formal or covenantal sense. Both sentences are true, and you cannot hold one without the other and tell the truth.

The shaping is undeniable. The moral imagination, the language of rights, the suspicion of concentrated power, the very idea that conscience is sacred, all of it came down from centuries of the church. The historian Mark Noll and the historian John Fea have both said it carefully. The culture was saturated with Christianity, and that saturation is written into the country down to its instincts. To deny it is to misread the evidence on the page.

But shaping a culture is not signing a covenant. The founders did not establish a Christian state. They built a secular government on purpose, a government with no creed and no test, designed to make room for the skeptic and the dissenter and the Jew and the unbeliever as full citizens. They did this not because they despised faith but because many of them, having watched established religion corrupt both throne and altar, believed that a faith protected by the sword is a faith already dying. Not a Christian nation. A nation deeply marked by Christians who refused to make it one. That distinction is the whole truth, and most of the shouting exists to avoid it.

And underneath the shouting sits an older hunger, one the first disciples felt before any of us. On the day he left them they asked the risen Jesus a single question, Lord, will you at this time restore the kingdom to Israel. They wanted a nation back. They wanted the map redrawn and the throne re-occupied and the enemy driven out. He did not give them the nation. What he gave them instead is the thing the whole American argument keeps stepping around.

sections.title: The Deeper Point
sections.body:
Here is where I have to turn the indictment on myself and on the church I love. The hunger to call America a Christian nation is rarely a hunger for accurate history. It is a hunger for a homeland that the New Testament refuses to give us. We want to be the chosen people, the city on the hill, the new Israel with a deed to the land. And every time we have claimed that mantle, we have used it to bless what God did not bless, to baptize conquest, to sanctify slavery, to make the cross a banner over our own power.

No nation is the new Israel, and the reason sits in that question on the mountain. Will you at this time restore the kingdom to Israel. It is the most natural question in the world, and Jesus refuses its premise. He does not correct the timing. He moves the whole hope to another plane. It is not for you to know the times, he tells them, but you will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you, and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and Judea and Samaria and to the ends of the earth. Read it slowly. The longing for a restored nation is not granted and rescheduled. It is answered with the Spirit and with a mission that runs past every border the disciples could name. The old Israel had a land because it was a sign pointing forward. The thing it pointed to arrived in a Galilean carpenter, executed by an empire that imagined it was eternal, and after him the people of God are gathered out of every nation and bound to none. That is why there is no successor state and never will be. To make a country the bearer of that promise is not patriotism. It is idolatry with a flag.

Name what is actually being mourned. When Christians say the country is turning against them, what is slipping is not the gospel. It is deference. The Pledge has said 'under God' since 1954. The currency has read 'In God We Trust' since 1956. In 1965, in 1975, in 1985, a Christian could walk through ordinary American life and never once be asked to defend what he believed. It was just the air. The air has changed, and we have mistaken a change in the weather for an attack on the faith. The gospel never needed that influence. The church only got used to it.

And here is the harder word, the one I have to say about my own side. The danger is not mainly that the church is being attacked from the outside. American Christianity is not being persecuted. It is being seduced, and seduction is worse, because seduction lets you keep everything. It lets you keep God and power, worship and control, the cross and the seat at the table. We reached for the country when we should have reached for the cross, and then we blamed the world for the emptiness we built ourselves. We did this. And we blamed that.

There is a way to love this country that does not lie about it. You can hold the genuine Christian fingerprints on its founding and still refuse to ask it to be a church. The myth was never protection. It is corrosion, because a kingdom that needs a nation has already forgotten that its King reigns without one. The church does not require America to be Christian. What America requires, and has always required, is a church that remembers it is not the kingdom, a church that took the answer on the mountain seriously and stopped waiting for the map to be redrawn. The day we forget that is the day we lose both the country and the cross.
